passage: On a hot Sunday in their Nagpur flat, Tushar, fifteen, sat through a documentary his sister Pallavi had put on, about a woman who spent forty years planting a forest on bare land by herself. He'd meant to watch ten minutes. He watched all of it. When the camera showed the trees she'd planted as saplings, now taller than houses, his throat went tight. That night he couldn't sleep. The next morning he carried three empty paint buckets to the terrace, filled them with soil, and planted neem seeds. Pallavi found him up there, dirt on his hands. "You're serious?" "Forty years," he said. "I've got time."

qa.q: What did Tushar plant in the paint buckets?
qa.a: Neem seeds.

qa.q: What was Tushar feeling when his throat went tight?
qa.a: He felt deeply moved and inspired by what one person's patience had built.

qa.q: What would help Tushar turn this feeling into a lasting project?
qa.a: Start small, learn how to care for the saplings, and maybe find a local tree-planting group to join.

qa.q: How might Pallavi see her brother's sudden project?
qa.a: She's surprised, maybe a bit amused, but might also feel proud that the film touched him.

grounding: Shows a teenager deeply moved by a role model's story and motivated to act.

passage:
"So, how was the concert, Simran?" asked her uncle Naveen as they walked to the bus stop.
"I can't talk yet."
"That good?"
"Chachu, the violinist closed her eyes for the slow part, and the whole hall went silent. I stopped breathing."
"You play the violin too."
"Not like that. I play notes. She played… feelings." Simran, sixteen, hugged her arms. "I want to practise properly. Not for exams. For that."
"That's a lot of practice."
"I know. Two hours a day?"
"Start with one," Naveen said. "And we'll find you a teacher who plays like that."

qa.q: What did the violinist do during the slow part?
qa.a: She closed her eyes.

qa.q: What does Simran saying "I can't talk yet" suggest?
qa.a: She felt so moved and overwhelmed by the music that she needed time before speaking.

qa.q: What did Naveen suggest, and why was it wise?
qa.a: Starting with one hour and finding a good teacher, because it turns inspiration into a sustainable plan.

qa.q: How might Naveen feel seeing Simran so moved?
qa.a: Warm and glad he took her, seeing the concert light something in her.

grounding: Shows a teenager deeply moved by a musician and motivated to practise for its own sake.

passage: I'm Simran. When I was fourteen, our Hindi teacher, Samir Sir, read a poem aloud about a mother waiting at a railway station for a son who never came back. He didn't explain it. He just read it slowly and then was quiet. I remember the dust in the light from the window. I went home and read it five more times. I didn't know words could hold that much. That weekend I wrote my first poem, badly, about my grandmother. I still write every week. Sometimes I think I became who I am because Sir decided not to explain that poem.

qa.q: What was the poem about?
qa.a: A mother waiting at a railway station for a son who never came back.

qa.q: How did Simran feel after hearing the poem?
qa.a: Simran felt deeply moved and amazed that words could hold so much feeling.

qa.q: What turning point does Simran describe?
qa.a: Samir Sir reading the poem and staying quiet instead of explaining it, which led to the first poem the next weekend.

qa.q: Why might Samir Sir have chosen not to explain the poem?
qa.a: Perhaps he trusted the students to feel it for themselves, knowing explanation might dull its power.

grounding: Shows a teenager looking back on being deeply moved by a poem and inspired to write.

passage:
"Didi, you've drawn his name on your hand again."
"Divyansh, go away."
"Arjit this, Arjit that. What's so special?"
Sarita, fifteen, sighed dreamily. "He's perfect. He helped a stray dog out of the drain. He reads poetry. He has the kindest eyes."
"Have you talked to him?"
"Once. He said 'excuse me' in the corridor."
"That's it?"
"The way he said it, though."
"He also picks his nose in maths."
"He does not!"
"Does. I sit behind him in tuition."
Sarita threw a pillow at him, but she went quiet afterwards, rubbing the ink off her hand.

qa.q: What did Sarita draw on her hand?
qa.a: His name, Arjit.

qa.q: What does Sarita calling Arjit "perfect" after one conversation suggest?
qa.a: She is infatuated, idealising him and filling in the gaps with what she hopes he is.

qa.q: What would you advise Sarita about her crush?
qa.a: It's okay to have strong feelings, but getting to know Arjit as a real person would show who he actually is.

qa.q: How does Divyansh see his sister's crush?
qa.a: He finds it silly and teases her, but his detail makes her think.

grounding: Shows a teenager's intense, idealised crush on a boy she barely knows.

passage: I'm Aparna, and at sixteen I was completely sure I was in love with my friend Sonali's older brother. He was in college. He played guitar on their balcony, and I'd find reasons to visit. I wrote pages in my diary about his hands, his laugh, how he'd once handed me a glass of water. I imagined whole conversations. Then one day I heard him arguing with Sonali about who'd finish the milk, just like any brother. I laughed so hard I had to leave. The feeling didn't vanish at once, but I began to see him as a person, not a poster.

qa.q: What did Sonali's brother play on the balcony?
qa.a: Guitar.

qa.q: How did Aparna feel while writing pages about him?
qa.a: Aparna felt swept up and dreamy, full of intense, idealised feelings.

qa.q: What turning point helped Aparna see him more clearly?
qa.a: Hearing him argue with Sonali about milk, which showed he was an ordinary person.

qa.q: How might Sonali have seen Aparna's frequent visits?
qa.a: She might have noticed and been amused, or wondered if she was the real reason Aparna came.

grounding: Shows a teenager looking back on an idealised crush and the moment it became more realistic.

passage:
Class teacher's note, Sangeeta, February
Kishore (15) has been distracted for two weeks. His notebook margins are full of one girl's initials, and he looks towards the next section whenever the door opens. His friends say he's written her a long letter but won't send it. I didn't mention it directly. I asked how he was, and he said, "I can't think about anything else." I told him strong feelings are normal and asked him to keep one hour a day for study. I'll keep an eye on his marks and check in again next week.

qa.q: What fills Kishore's notebook margins?
qa.a: One girl's initials.

qa.q: What does Kishore saying "I can't think about anything else" suggest?
qa.a: He is infatuated, caught up in intense and consuming feelings.

qa.q: Why was Sangeeta's approach sensible?
qa.a: She respected his privacy, told him the feelings are normal and gave him a simple structure for study.

qa.q: How might Kishore's friends see his unsent letter?
qa.a: They might tease him, or be curious whether he'll ever send it.

grounding: Shows a teenager consumed by an intense crush, noticed by his class teacher.

passage:
Hansa: he said no
Sumit: who? Kunal?? to the farewell?
Hansa: yeah. in front of everyone
Hansa: said he's going with his friends
Sumit: oh Hansa. that's rough 😔
Hansa: i feel so stupid. my chest actually hurts
Sumit: girl, you're not stupid. you took a risk
Hansa: everyone laughed
Sumit: some people laughed. i didn't. neither did most
Hansa: i can't face school tomorrow
Sumit: then we walk in together. i'll wait at your gate at 7.30

Hansa: maybe. thanks Sumit 🤍

qa.q: What time did Sumit say he would wait at the gate?
What does Hansa saying "my chest actually hurts" suggest?
qa.a: She feels overwhelming hurt and embarrassment after being turned down in front of everyone.

qa.q: What did Sumit do that helped?
qa.a: He listened, told Hansa she wasn't stupid, offered to walk in together and suggested talking to her mum.

qa.q: How might Kunal feel if he noticed everyone laughing?
qa.a: He might feel uncomfortable or sorry, especially if he didn't mean to hurt her publicly.

grounding: Shows a teenager's acute pain after a public romantic rejection and a friend helping her through it.

passage: In the small town, the bus stop was the only place to talk privately. Jyoti, seventeen, had finally told the boy from her coaching class how she felt. He'd looked at the road and said, "I don't feel that way. Sorry." The bus came. She got on and sat at the back. Her friend Sabina sat beside her and didn't say anything for three stops. Then Jyoti whispered, "It hurts everywhere." Sabina held her hand. At home, Jyoti's mother noticed her red eyes and made ginger tea without asking questions. That night Jyoti cried into her pillow, but she woke up still breathing, still herself.

qa.q: Where did Jyoti tell the boy how she felt?
qa.a: At the bus stop.

qa.q: What was Jyoti feeling when she whispered "It hurts everywhere"?
qa.a: She felt overwhelmed and heartbroken by the rejection.

qa.q: What made Sabina's support helpful?
qa.a: She stayed close and quiet, letting Jyoti feel the pain without pressure to talk.

qa.q: How might Jyoti's mother see her red eyes?
qa.a: She understands something hurt her daughter and chooses gentle care over questions.

grounding: Shows a teenager processing the overwhelming pain of romantic rejection, supported by her friend and mother.

passage: In a flat in Copenhagen, Bilal, sixteen, read Ulla's message three times: "I think we should just be friends. I'm sorry." They'd been together four months. He put the phone face down, then picked it up again. He didn't go to football. He didn't eat dinner. His father knocked on his door at nine and sat on the edge of the bed. "Bad day?" Bilal's voice cracked. "She ended it." His father nodded slowly. "That hurts like nothing else at your age. Want to walk?" They walked to the harbour in the cold and didn't talk much. Bilal came back tired, but less alone.

qa.q: How long had Bilal and Ulla been together?
qa.a: Four months.

qa.q: What does Bilal skipping football and dinner suggest?
qa.a: He was overwhelmed and heartbroken, too hurt to carry on as normal.

qa.q: Which choice by Bilal's father helped, and why?
qa.a: Sitting with him and offering a walk, because it gave comfort without forcing him to talk.

qa.q: How might Ulla be feeling after sending the message?
qa.a: She may feel sad or guilty too, even if she believed it was the right decision.

grounding: Shows a teenager processing the acute pain of a breakup with his father's quiet support.

passage: "Seema, you think you have to be strong all the time? When I, your Omkar Mama, was sixteen, I had a stammer, worst on words starting with 'p'. I never talked in groups. My friends thought I was just quiet. One evening on the riverbank, my friend Sadanand asked why I never told stories. My heart was hammering. I could have made a joke. Instead I said, slowly, 'Because I'm scared of getting stuck in front of you.' He didn't laugh. He said, 'Then get stuck. We'll wait.' That was the first time I told a story in front of anyone."

qa.q: Which words did young Omkar's stammer affect most?
qa.a: Words starting with 'p'.

qa.q: What was young Omkar feeling when his heart was hammering?
qa.a: He felt scared and exposed, afraid of being judged if he told the truth.

qa.q: What turning point in the story came from opening up?
qa.a: Admitting his fear instead of joking, which led Sadanand to offer patience.

qa.q: How might Sadanand have felt when Omkar opened up?
qa.a: Touched and trusted, and glad to understand why his friend stayed quiet.

grounding: Shows an elder recalling how as a teenager he took the risk of opening up about his stammer to a friend.

passage: The bus to school was packed, horns blaring outside, and Lakshmi, sixteen, had to shout to be heard. She'd been rehearsing this for weeks. "Anirban, can I tell you something?" He leaned closer. "Since we moved here, I've felt lonely all the time. Even when I'm laughing with the group. I pretend I'm fine." She stared at the window, scared of his face. The bus jolted. Anirban was quiet for a moment. "I had no idea," he said. "Thank you for telling me. Want to get chai after school? Just us, so we can actually talk." Lakshmi nodded, her eyes stinging.

qa.q: Where did Lakshmi tell Anirban?
qa.a: On the packed bus to school.

qa.q: Why did Lakshmi stare at the window after speaking?
qa.a: She felt vulnerable and afraid of how Anirban would react to her honesty.

qa.q: What did Anirban do that honoured her risk?
qa.a: He thanked her and offered a quiet time to talk properly after school.

qa.q: How might Anirban feel learning his friend was lonely?
qa.a: Surprised and concerned, and glad she trusted him with it.

grounding: Shows a teenager taking the risk of admitting loneliness to a friend in a noisy, crowded place.

passage: Kavitha, seventeen, had told everyone the entrance exam went "fine". It hadn't. At the colony park bench, her friend Bhavna asked for the third time, "Really fine?" Kavitha's hands were cold. She could keep pretending, or she could say it. "I think I failed. And I'm scared that if I'm not an engineer, my parents will be disappointed in me for ever." She hadn't said those words even to herself. Bhavna didn't rush to fix it. "That sounds so heavy," she said. "Thank you for telling me." Kavitha cried, and felt lighter than she had in months.

qa.q: What had Kavitha told everyone about the exam?
qa.a: That it went "fine".

qa.q: What was Kavitha feeling as her hands went cold?
qa.a: She felt anxious and exposed, weighing whether to risk telling the truth.

qa.q: What would you advise Kavitha next?
qa.a: Share the same fears with her parents or a school counsellor, now that she's said them out loud once.

qa.q: How might Bhavna feel when Kavitha finally opens up?
qa.a: Trusted and caring, and relieved her friend stopped pretending.

grounding: Shows a teenager taking the risk of opening up fully to a friend about her fears.

passage: In the small town, the board exams were a week away, and Irawati, sixteen, woke at four with her heart racing. She'd read that breathing slowly helped, so she lay still and counted: in for four, hold for four, out for six. It helped a little. At dawn she laced up her shoes and ran three rounds of the school ground, feet slapping, lungs burning. Her younger brother Jatin found her stretching by the gate. "Running before an exam?" "It empties my head," she said. The next morning he came too. By exam day, she still felt nervous, but it no longer swallowed her.

qa.q: How many rounds of the school ground did Irawati run?
qa.a: Three rounds.

qa.q: What was Irawati feeling when she woke at four with her heart racing?
qa.a: She felt anxious and panicky about the upcoming exams.

qa.q: Why are Irawati's breathing and running useful habits?
qa.a: They calm her body so her mind can settle, giving her some control over the anxiety.

qa.q: How might Jatin see his sister's dawn runs?
qa.a: First as strange, then as something worth trying, since he joins her.

grounding: Shows a teenager using breathing and exercise to manage exam anxiety.

passage: The night before her piano recital in Kyoto, Yuki, fifteen, sat on her bed with her hands shaking so badly she couldn't hold a cup. Her friend Jamal, visiting from next door, noticed. "My swimming coach taught me this," he said. "Press your feet flat on the floor. Breathe out longer than you breathe in." Yuki tried it. Five breaths. Ten. Her hands slowed. "Now walk with me round the block." They walked in the cool air, not talking. When she came back, she played the piece once through, softly, and went to sleep. At the recital her hands still trembled a little, but they played.

qa.q: How many breaths did Yuki take before her hands slowed?
qa.a: Ten breaths.

qa.q: What was Yuki feeling when her hands shook?
qa.a: She felt highly anxious and nervous about the recital.

qa.q: What did Jamal's suggestions do well?
qa.a: They gave her simple body-based steps, grounding and slow breathing, then a calm walk.

qa.q: How might Jamal feel seeing Yuki calm down?
qa.a: Relieved and glad his coach's trick worked for his friend.

grounding: Shows a teenager using breathwork and walking to calm performance anxiety with a friend's help.

passage: Before the inter-school debate final, Pema, sixteen, hid in the girls' changing room of the sports complex, breathing fast. Her PE teacher, Sonali Ma'am, found her there. "Talk to me." "I can't breathe properly. My mind's blank." Sonali crouched down. "Shake your hands out, hard. Now roll your shoulders. Good. Breathe in through your nose, slowly, and out through your mouth, like blowing a candle." Pema did it five times. Her shoulders dropped. "Better?" "A bit." "Then walk to the stage with me." Pema stood. Her legs were still wobbly, but she walked.

qa.q: Where did Pema hide before the final?
qa.a: In the girls' changing room of the sports complex.

qa.q: What was Pema feeling when her mind went blank?
qa.a: She felt overwhelmed with anxiety and panic before the debate.

qa.q: Which of Sonali Ma'am's steps helped most, and why?
qa.a: Shaking out and slow breathing, because they calmed Pema's body so she could think again.

qa.q: How might Sonali Ma'am feel as Pema walks to the stage?
qa.a: Relieved and proud that Pema used the steps and faced her fear.

grounding: Shows a teenager using physical self-calming strategies, guided by a teacher, to handle anxiety before a debate.

passage: First week of term: the new rule said girls couldn't play football at recess, "for safety". Gurleen, fifteen, was furious but said nothing. Second week: she asked her friend Siddharth, "What's unsafe about us that isn't unsafe about you?" He didn't have an answer. She wrote down both sides, and some of her own arguments were weaker than she'd thought. Third week: she took a calm letter to the principal, signed by twenty girls and boys, asking for a trial week. The principal agreed. "It's not about football," Gurleen told Siddharth. "It's about rules having reasons."

qa.q: How many students signed the letter?
qa.a: Twenty girls and boys.

qa.q: What was Gurleen feeling in the first week?
qa.a: She was furious at a rule that seemed unfair, but not yet ready to act.

qa.q: What made Gurleen's challenge effective?
qa.a: She questioned the rule, tested her own arguments and then made a calm, reasoned request.

qa.q: How might Siddharth see Gurleen's question?
qa.a: It probably made him think, since he couldn't find a good answer.

grounding: Shows a teenager challenging an arbitrary rule and defining her own sense of fairness over three weeks.

passage: "Vikas, you ask why I never cared who sat where at weddings. When I, your Abhinav Dada, was sixteen, our village feast had separate rows for different families, as it always had. My friend Ramu, the potter's son, was put far away. I stood there with my plate, thinking: my father says all people are equal before God, so why these rows? If I sat with Ramu, my father would be shamed. If I didn't, I'd be a hypocrite. My hands were sweating. I walked over and sat beside Ramu. My father didn't speak to me for two days. Then, at the next feast, he came and sat with us too."

qa.q: Where did young Abhinav sit at the feast?
qa.a: Beside Ramu, the potter's son.

qa.q: What was young Abhinav feeling when his hands were sweating?
qa.a: He felt torn and afraid, caught between loyalty to his father and his own sense of right.

qa.q: What turning point in the story changed the father?
qa.a: Abhinav choosing to sit beside Ramu, which later led his father to join them.

qa.q: How might Ramu have felt when Abhinav sat beside him?
qa.a: Surprised and respected, perhaps moved that his friend took the risk.

grounding: Shows an elder recalling how as a teenager he challenged an unfair custom and defined his own moral compass.

passage: Nazia, sixteen, and her cousin Zainab found a wallet on the way home from tuition: an ID card and two thousand rupees. Nazia's family had been short of money for months; her father's shop was barely running. Zainab whispered, "Nobody saw." Nazia felt the notes in her fingers. "Keeping it would help Abbu." "But it's someone else's Abbu's money." They argued all the way home. Nazia thought: if I lost this, I'd want it back. And if I keep it because I'm poorer, does that make it right? They took it to the address on the ID. A tired nurse opened the door and cried with relief.

qa.q: What was inside the wallet?
qa.a: An ID card and two thousand rupees.

qa.q: What was Nazia feeling as she held the notes?
qa.a: She felt tempted and torn, knowing the money could help her family but that it wasn't theirs.

qa.q: What reasoning helped Nazia decide?
qa.a: Imagining losing it herself, and questioning whether being poorer made keeping it right.

qa.q: How might the nurse have felt opening the door?
qa.a: Relieved and grateful, probably having feared the money was gone.

grounding: Shows a teenager wrestling with an ethical dilemma under money pressure and deciding by her own moral compass.

passage: Sachin, thanks for having me on the school podcast. So, I'm Jatin, Class 11. Last month, in the canteen, some seniors were mocking a boy for his lunch, calling it smelly, filming him. Everyone laughed or looked away. I nearly did too. Then I thought about my little brother, and I walked over, sat next to the boy and said, 'Smells great, actually. Can I try?' The seniors turned on me. Someone called me a loser. That afternoon I went with the boy to our class teacher and told her what happened and about the video. She called the seniors in the same day. People still tease me a bit. I'd do it again.

qa.q: What were the seniors doing to the boy?
qa.a: Mocking him for his lunch, calling it smelly and filming him.

qa.q: What was Jatin feeling when he decided to walk over?
qa.a: Jatin felt nervous but protective, unwilling to join the crowd against the boy.

qa.q: What made Jatin's response effective?
qa.a: Jatin supported the boy on the spot and, the same day, took the matter to the class teacher with the boy.

qa.q: How might the bullied boy have felt when Jatin sat beside him?
qa.a: Relieved and less alone, finally with someone on his side.

grounding: Shows a teenager standing up for a bullied peer despite social risk and getting adult help the same day.

passage: I'm Maria, and I sit near Farhan in Class 10. Last week someone posted an edited photo of a new boy in our class group, with a cruel caption. Messages flew. Laughing emojis everywhere. Farhan, fifteen, typed: "This isn't funny. Delete it." For a minute nobody replied. Then someone wrote, "Chill, bro," and a few people left the group. Farhan didn't back down. At lunch he went to our class teacher with a screenshot, and the photo was gone by the evening. I don't know if he was scared, but I saw his hands shake while he typed.

qa.q: What did Farhan type in the class group?
qa.a: "This isn't funny. Delete it."

qa.q: What might Farhan have felt as his hands shook while typing?
qa.a: He was probably nervous but determined, knowing speaking up was risky.

qa.q: What made Farhan's actions effective?
qa.a: He spoke up in the group and took the screenshot to the teacher the same day.

qa.q: How does Maria see Farhan's courage?
qa.a: Maria noticed his shaking hands and seems to respect that he spoke up anyway.

grounding: Shows a teenager standing up for a peer targeted online despite social risk, seen by a classmate.

passage: Monday: a new girl, Sabina, joined Class 9, and some girls started whispering about her clothes. Ritu, fourteen, noticed but stayed quiet, afraid she'd be next. Wednesday: the whispers turned into a nickname, shouted across the corridor. Sabina ate lunch alone. Ritu's stomach twisted. She picked up her tiffin and sat with Sabina. "Mind if I sit here?" That afternoon Ritu went to her class teacher and told her about the nickname; the teacher spoke to the girls before the last bell. Friday: two other girls joined their table. The nickname faded, though Ritu lost one friend over it.

qa.q: What did the girls whisper about?
qa.a: Sabina's clothes.

qa.q: What was Ritu feeling when her stomach twisted?
qa.a: She felt guilty and uneasy watching Sabina eat alone, torn between fear and doing what was right.

qa.q: Which choices by Ritu made a difference?
qa.a: Sitting with Sabina and telling the class teacher the same afternoon, so an adult acted quickly.

qa.q: How might Sabina have felt when Ritu sat down?
qa.a: Relieved and less alone, after days of isolation.

grounding: Shows a teenager moving from silence to standing up for a bullied peer, despite the social cost.

passage: On the terrace of their Pune building, Tushar, sixteen, lay on a mat beside his grandmother Madhuri, watching stars. "Aaji, what do you think we're here for?" She didn't answer right away. "When I was your age, I thought it was to do my duty. Later, I thought it was to love my children. Now I think it's to pay attention." "To what?" "To this." She pointed at the sky, then at him. Tushar was quiet. He'd been reading about the universe, how tiny Earth was, and it frightened him. But lying there, it felt less like being tiny and more like being part of something. He wrote her words in his phone's notes that night.

qa.q: Where were Tushar and his grandmother lying?
qa.a: On the terrace of their Pune building.

qa.q: How did Tushar's feeling about being tiny change?
qa.a: It went from frightening to feeling connected, as if he was part of something bigger.

qa.q: What might help Tushar keep exploring these questions?
qa.a: Keep talking with people like Aaji, reading widely and writing down his own thoughts.

qa.q: How might Aaji Madhuri feel about Tushar's question?
qa.a: Touched and glad, seeing him think deeply about life.

grounding: Shows a teenager exploring questions of meaning and connection with his grandmother.

passage:
"Kavitha, do you ever feel like the hills are listening?"
"Lalremsiami, it's six in the morning. I feel like sleeping."
"I'm serious." Lalremsiami, sixteen, pulled her shawl tighter. "At church, I feel close to God. But up here, I feel it too, and there's no church."
"Maybe God's not only in buildings."
"You don't even believe in a God."
"I believe in something," Kavitha said. "When my grandmother died, I felt like she went back into everything. The trees, the rain."
"That's beautiful."
"So maybe we're both looking at the same thing from different sides."
They watched the mist lift off the valley, and neither spoke for a long time.

qa.q: What did Lalremsiami pull tighter?
qa.a: Her shawl.

qa.q: What was Lalremsiami feeling on the hill?
qa.a: She felt a deep sense of closeness and wonder, as if connected to something beyond herself.

qa.q: What made this conversation work despite their different beliefs?
qa.a: Both listened with respect and looked for what they shared rather than who was right.

qa.q: How might Kavitha feel sharing her thoughts about her grandmother?
qa.a: Tender and a bit exposed, but glad Lalremsiami found it beautiful.

grounding: Shows two teenagers exploring spiritual questions and universal connection from different beliefs.

passage: I'm Ritu. When I was seventeen, I went on a trek with my school to a village in the hills, and our guide was an old farmer named Bhupen. On the last night I asked him if he ever wondered what life was for. He laughed. "Every morning," he said. "Then I water the apple trees." I thought it was a joke. But on the long bus home I kept thinking about it: maybe meaning isn't one big answer, but what you choose to care for each day. I started keeping a notebook of questions I didn't have answers to. It's still growing.

qa.q: What does Bhupen do every morning after wondering?
qa.a: He waters the apple trees.

qa.q: How did Ritu feel about Bhupen's answer at first?
qa.a: Ritu thought it was a joke and felt a little puzzled, before it began to feel meaningful.

qa.q: What turning point shaped Ritu's personal philosophy?
qa.a: Thinking about Bhupen's answer on the bus, and seeing meaning as daily care rather than one big answer.

qa.q: How might Bhupen have seen Ritu's question?
qa.a: With amusement and kindness, as a question he still lives with himself.

grounding: Shows a teenager exploring questions of meaning and forming a personal philosophy after a conversation with a farmer.

passage:
Reena's diary, Saturday
Third week of teaching the kids at the community hall. They're children of the construction workers building the tower next door, and most have never had a proper notebook. Omkar and I brought chart paper and crayons. Today a boy, maybe eight, read a whole sentence alone and looked at me like he'd climbed a mountain. On the way out, a guy from our class passed and said, "Doing charity for selfies?" Omkar laughed it off. I didn't. I told him the kids have names, and they deserve better than jokes. He went quiet. I'm tired, but I've never felt more useful.

qa.q: What did Reena and Omkar bring?
qa.a: Chart paper and crayons.

qa.q: How did Reena feel after the boy read his first sentence?
qa.a: Reena felt proud and deeply useful, moved by his achievement.

qa.q: What would you advise Reena about the classmate's comment?

passage: In the small town, the ration office was always crowded with elderly people who couldn't read the forms. Chetan, seventeen, started going there on Saturdays with a pen and a folding stool, filling forms for anyone who asked. His classmate Tenzin, whose family came from a Tibetan settlement nearby, joined him. One Saturday a man in the queue told Tenzin, "Outsiders shouldn't be helping here." Chetan put down his pen. "He was born two streets away, uncle. Same as me." The man grumbled but let Tenzin fill his form. Afterwards Tenzin said, "You didn't have to." Chetan shrugged. "Yes, I did."

passage: Vidya, you want the scooter story for your project? Fine. I'm Jagdish, I was seventeen. It was midnight after a wedding, and my friends wanted to ride three on one scooter, no helmets, to the highway dhaba. Everyone was loud, laughing, daring me. I had the keys. My heart was going fast and I wanted to say yes so badly. Then I remembered what our PE sir said: when you're hot, wait ten minutes before you decide. So I said I needed the bathroom and stood there, counting. When I came back, I said no. They called me boring. Two of them walked home with me anyway.

qa.q: What was Jagdish feeling when holding the keys?
qa.a: Jagdish felt excited, pressured and tempted, with a racing heart.

qa.q: Which choice made the difference, and why?

qa.q: How might the two friends who walked home with Jagdish have felt?

grounding: Shows a teenager learning to delay a risky decision made under excitement and peer pressure.

passage: I'm Kiran, Jeevan's teammate. In Saturday's match, a boy from the other side slid in hard and caught Jeevan's ankle on purpose. Jeevan, sixteen, jumped up, fists clenched, face red, and took two steps towards him. Everyone froze. Then he stopped, turned round, and walked to the touchline. He stood there with his hands on his head, breathing hard. After a minute he came back and told the referee, calmly, what had happened. The boy got a yellow card. I don't know what went on in his head in those seconds, but it was the calmest I've seen him.

passage: Friday night: Manjula, fifteen, found out her friend Sunaina had told others about her crush. Furious, she typed a long message full of insults, finger over send. Instead she saved it as a draft and went to sleep, still angry. Saturday: she reread it. Some of it made her wince. She deleted half. Sunday: she met Sunaina in person. "I felt betrayed when you told everyone." Sunaina's face fell. "I thought it was a joke. I'm really sorry." Manjula was glad she hadn't sent the draft. The words she'd almost said would have been impossible to take back.

qa.q: What did Manjula do with the angry message on Friday night?
qa.a: She saved it as a draft and went to sleep.

qa.q: What was Manjula feeling when she reread the message on Saturday?
qa.a: She felt uncomfortable and a little ashamed at how harsh it was.

qa.q: What helped Manjula make a better choice?
qa.a: Waiting until she was calm and then speaking in person about how she felt.

qa.q: How might Sunaina have felt when Manjula spoke calmly?
qa.a: Guilty and sorry, and more able to apologise than if she'd been attacked.

grounding: Shows a teenager over a weekend learning to hold back a choice made in anger and respond more coolly.
